description: Police powers, the judiciary, magistrates, juries and legal representatives explained.
content_html:
The Role of the Police

The police are responsible for maintaining law and order, preventing and investigating crime, and protecting the public. In England and Wales, policing is carried out by territorial forces, each overseen by an elected police and crime commissioner. The commissioner is accountable to local communities and can influence police budgets and strategic direction.

Police officers have significant powers, but these are balanced against citizens’ rights. Officers may stop and search a person if they have reasonable grounds to suspect the individual is carrying weapons, stolen goods or articles for use in crime. They may arrest someone they reasonably suspect has committed, is committing or is about to commit an offence. Once arrested, a person must be informed of the reason for their arrest and their right to legal advice.

Key Fact

Police powers are balanced against citizens’ rights. The police may stop and search only when they have reasonable grounds to suspect someone of carrying weapons, stolen goods or items for use in crime.

Supporters of stop and search argue that the power is a vital tool for reducing serious knife and gun crime, particularly in urban areas. They contend that targeted searches can remove weapons from the streets before violence occurs, and that officers need the flexibility to act on intelligence.

Critics argue that stop and search has been applied disproportionately against certain communities, especially Black and mixed-heritage individuals, without sufficient justification. They contend this undermines community trust in the police and does not reliably reduce crime. Official statistics from the Home Office show that Black people were stopped and searched at a significantly higher rate than white people in 2022–23. The debate reflects a wider tension between effective policing and the protection of civil liberties.

Courts in England and Wales

The court system is divided into criminal courts and civil courts, each operating at different levels. In criminal cases, less serious offences (summary offences) are heard in the Magistrates’ Court, while more serious crimes (indictable offences) go to the Crown Court. Appeals from the Crown Court may eventually reach the Court of Appeal and, in exceptional cases, the Supreme Court.

Civil disputes — such as contract disagreements, personal injury claims and property disputes — are heard in the County Court for lower-value claims and the High Court for complex or high-value cases. Tribunals handle specialist areas such as employment grievances, immigration and tax matters. They are generally quicker and less formal than courts, making justice more accessible to ordinary citizens.

Key Fact

Criminal courts in England and Wales include the Magistrates’ Court (summary offences) and the Crown Court (indictable offences). Civil disputes go to the County Court or the High Court. Tribunals resolve specialist disputes such as employment cases.

Magistrates and the Magistrates’ Court

Magistrates are volunteer lay justices who hear around 95% of all criminal cases in England and Wales. They are members of the public, not legally qualified judges, though they receive training and are advised on points of law by a court legal adviser. A typical bench consists of three magistrates. Magistrates can impose fines, community sentences and custodial sentences of up to six months for a single offence (or twelve months for multiple offences). Serious cases they cannot deal with are sent up to the Crown Court.

The advantages of lay magistrates include the fact that justice is delivered by ordinary community members rather than a legal elite, reducing costs compared with jury trials. Critics point out that magistrates may lack consistency across different areas and that conviction rates in the Magistrates’ Court are high, raising questions about whether defendants always receive a sufficiently rigorous hearing.

Juries and the Crown Court

A jury consists of twelve randomly selected members of the public aged 18–70 who are registered to vote. Juries hear the evidence presented by both prosecution and defence in Crown Court trials and then retire to reach a verdict. A unanimous verdict is preferred, but a majority verdict (ten of twelve) may be accepted by the judge in certain circumstances. The jury decides only on matters of fact — whether the defendant is guilty — while the judge rules on matters of law and determines the sentence if a guilty verdict is returned.

A common misconception is that the judge decides whether a defendant is guilty or not guilty. In a Crown Court trial, it is the jury that decides guilt — the twelve members of the public who have heard all the evidence. The judge’s role is to manage the trial fairly, rule on points of law, direct the jury on the legal standard they must apply, and — if a guilty verdict is returned — to decide the sentence. In a Magistrates’ Court there is no jury, so magistrates decide both verdict and sentence.

The Judiciary

Judges are legally qualified professionals who manage trials, interpret the law and, in civil cases, make decisions on liability and awards. In England and Wales, judges are appointed on merit through the independent Judicial Appointments Commission, which safeguards judicial independence. This independence is vital in a democracy — citizens must be confident that courts are not influenced by the government of the day. In criminal cases, circuit judges and recorders hear cases in the Crown Court; High Court judges deal with the most serious matters.

Legal Representatives

Citizens involved in legal proceedings may be represented by qualified legal professionals. A solicitor advises clients on their legal rights, prepares cases and may represent clients in lower courts. A barrister is a specialist court advocate who presents cases in the Crown Court and higher courts. Barristers are typically instructed by solicitors on behalf of clients. Citizens who cannot afford legal representation may apply for legal aid, which is state-funded assistance for those who meet the financial criteria.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe question about courts or legal representatives, give two clearly developed points — for example, name a specific court and explain the type of case it handles. Avoid just listing terms without development. For 8-mark Analyse questions, you must present two sides of the argument (for example, arguments for and against lay magistrates or jury trials) and reach a substantiated judgement. One-sided answers are capped in the Developing band. For 12-mark Evaluate, make sure your conclusion adds a reasoned overall judgement, not just a summary: explain why one side of the argument is more convincing, and name a real-world example (the Magistrates’ Court handling 95% of cases, judicial independence through the Judicial Appointments Commission) to lift your answer into the Mastering band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The police have powers of stop and search and arrest, but these are balanced against citizens’ rights; police and crime commissioners hold chief constables to account.
  • Criminal courts range from the Magistrates’ Court (summary offences, lay justices) to the Crown Court (serious crimes, judge and jury); civil courts include the County Court and the High Court; tribunals handle specialist disputes.
  • Juries decide guilt in Crown Court trials; judges manage the trial and sentence; solicitors advise and prepare cases; barristers advocate in higher courts; judicial independence is protected through the Judicial Appointments Commission.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following courts handles the most serious criminal cases in England and Wales?
A) Magistrates' Court
B) County Court
C) Crown Court
D) Employment Tribunal
Identify two roles carried out by a judge during a Crown Court trial.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two clearly distinct roles from the following:
- Managing the trial fairly and ruling on points of law
- Directing the jury on the legal standard they must apply (beyond reasonable doubt)
- Deciding the sentence if a guilty verdict is returned
- Advising on points of law (in Magistrates' Court context)
Do not credit two versions of the same role. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Magistrates' Court in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development).
- Magistrates are lay (unqualified) volunteers from the community who are trained and supported by a legal adviser (1 + 1).
- The Magistrates' Court handles summary (less serious) criminal offences and can impose fines, community orders and short custodial sentences of up to six months (1 + 1).
- Around 95% of all criminal cases in England and Wales are heard in the Magistrates' Court (1 + 1).
Do not credit evaluation or comparison — description only.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

A fictional broadsheet newspaper reported: 'A 2024 survey of 1,500 adults found that 62% believed ordinary people on juries are better placed than professional judges to decide questions of guilt, because they represent the public. However, 28% disagreed, arguing that jurors lack the legal knowledge to evaluate complex evidence fairly, while 10% were undecided.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain what the extract tells us about public attitudes towards jury trials.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: identification (1), interpretation (1), own knowledge (1), substantiated judgement (1).
- 1 mark for identifying what the source shows: a majority (62%) favour jury trial because they see juries as representative of the public.
- 1 mark for interpreting a key detail: nearly three in ten (28%) are sceptical, suggesting significant minority concern about jurors' legal competence.
- 1 mark for connecting to own knowledge: juries in England and Wales consist of twelve randomly selected registered voters aged 18-70 who must decide guilt to a criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
- 1 mark for a substantiated judgement: the source suggests majority public support for jury trials exists, but the level of disagreement (28%) indicates debate about whether lay decision-making produces consistent, legally informed verdicts.

practice_questions.text: Analyse whether the use of lay magistrates to decide criminal cases is an effective way of delivering justice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced two-sided analysis with at least one named real-world example on each side (e.g. 95% of cases handled by magistrates, Magistrates' Court sentencing powers, criticisms of inconsistency or high conviction rates). A substantiated judgement that weighs the two sides and reaches a clear conclusion about overall effectiveness.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most points present, generally accurate, two-sided in places. At least one named example. A concluding judgement present but not fully developed.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but limited development, or one-sided argument. Some reference to courts or sentencing but no named specific example. Little or no weighing of evidence.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about magistrates or courts; descriptive rather than analytical; no real-world example or judgement.

practice_questions.text: A local justice campaign group is calling for all criminal cases in England and Wales, including summary offences, to be decided by a judge alone rather than by lay magistrates or juries. Evaluate whether removing lay decision-makers from criminal courts would improve or damage justice in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument. Arguments for removing lay decision-makers (e.g. legal expertise, consistency, efficiency, reduced risk of jury bias) weighed against arguments for retaining them (democratic participation, community representation, public confidence, the principle that citizens are judged by peers, the Magistrates' Court's capacity handling 95% of cases). At least one named real-world example or institution on each side. A substantiated overall judgement in the conclusion that goes beyond 'it depends' and provides criteria for the judgement.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides covered, at least one named example, a judgement present but not fully substantiated.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some coverage of both sides but limited development; limited or no named examples; judgement weak or missing.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points; largely one-sided; no named examples; no evaluative conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the role of a police and crime commissioner?
options: To prosecute criminals in the Crown Court
To set policing priorities and hold the chief constable to account
To decide sentences in the Magistrates' Court
To represent defendants in criminal trials

knowledge_checks.q: In a Crown Court trial, who decides whether a defendant is guilty?
A barrister is a specialist _____ who presents cases in the Crown Court and higher courts.
Around _____ of all criminal cases in England and Wales are heard in the Magistrates' Court.
Match each legal term to its correct description:
right: A specialist panel resolving disputes in areas like employment or immigration
A lawyer who advises clients and prepares cases but does not usually appear in higher courts
A serious criminal offence tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of a police and crime commissioner?
flashcard_questions.a: An elected official who sets policing priorities and holds the chief constable to account.

flashcard_questions.q: Which court in England and Wales handles summary (less serious) criminal offences?
Which court handles serious (indictable) criminal offences such as murder?

flashcard_questions.a: A less serious criminal offence tried in the Magistrates' Court.

flashcard_questions.q: How many jurors sit on a jury in the Crown Court?
In a Crown Court trial, who decides guilt and who decides sentence?
flashcard_questions.a: The jury decides guilt; the judge decides the sentence.
The principle that judges decide cases on the law alone, free from political pressure.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a solicitor and a barrister?
flashcard_questions.a: Solicitors advise clients and prepare cases; barristers are court advocates in higher courts.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of disputes does an employment tribunal resolve?
flashcard_questions.a: Workplace grievances such as unfair dismissal, outside the main court system.
A volunteer lay justice who hears criminal cases in the Magistrates' Court.

flashcard_questions.q: What maximum custodial sentence can magistrates impose for a single offence?
What body safeguards judicial independence by appointing judges on merit?

flashcard_questions.a: A serious criminal offence tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury.

glossary_terms.definition: An elected official who sets the policing priorities for a local area and holds the chief constable to account.
A less serious criminal offence tried in the Magistrates' Court, such as minor theft, traffic violations and low-level assault.
A serious criminal offence such as murder, rape and serious fraud, which is tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury.
A specialist panel that resolves disputes in areas such as employment, immigration and tax, outside the main court system.
A group of twelve randomly selected members of the public who hear the evidence in a Crown Court trial and deliver a verdict of guilty or not guilty.
The principle that judges operate free from political pressure and decide cases purely on the basis of the law and the evidence before them.
A lawyer who advises clients, prepares legal documents and instructs barristers but does not normally appear in higher courts.
A specialist advocate who presents cases in court, particularly in the Crown Court and higher courts.
